q: In the four-party card model, what is the financial institution that provides card acceptance services to merchants called?
explain: A four-party system consists of the cardholder, the merchant, the acquiring bank and the issuing bank; the acquirer is the merchant's bank for card acceptance.
hook: Acquirer acquires merchants; issuer issues cards.

sources.title: Mastercard Interchange Fees and Rates Explained | Mastercard US
sources.quote: Financial institutions that provide card acceptance services to merchants are typically referred to as “acquirers”.

sources.title: Credit Card Swipe Fees and Routing Restrictions | Congress.gov
sources.quote: Four-party systems consist of the cardholder, the merchant, the acquiring bank, and the issuing bank. In a four-party system, the network connects merchants to issuing banks.

q: Which major card network uses a three-party model in which the network provider also acts as issuer and acquirer?
explain: In three-party (closed-loop) networks such as American Express, the network both issues cards and holds the acquiring relationship with merchants; Visa and Mastercard are four-party systems.
hook: AmEx closes the loop: one company on both ends.

sources.title: Merchant Discount, Interchange, and Other Transaction Fees in the Retail Electronic Payment System | Congress.gov
sources.quote: interchange fees are charged only in four-party networks such as Visa and Mastercard, where there is an issuing bank, an acquiring bank, a consumer, and a merchant. Alternatively, in three-party networks, such as American Express, the network provider's bank also acts as the issuer and acquirer.

sources.title: American Express Company 2017 Form 10-K - SEC.gov
sources.quote: Wherever we manage both the card-issuing activities of the business and the acquiring relationship with merchants, there is a “closed loop” in that we have direct access to information at both ends of the card transaction, which distinguishes our integrated network from the bankcard networks.

q: In Visa and Mastercard transactions, interchange fees are paid by the acquirer to which party?
explain: Interchange is generally paid by acquirers to card issuers; acquirers typically pass it through to merchants as part of the merchant discount rate.

sources.title: Mastercard Interchange Fees and Rates Explained | Mastercard US
sources.quote: Mastercard interchange rates are established by Mastercard, and are generally paid by acquirers to card issuers on purchase transactions conducted on Mastercard cards.

sources.title: PSR Card acquiring market review - Final report - Glossary
sources.quote: Interchange fee A fee that acquirers pay to issuers each time a card is used to buy goods or services.

q: What is the per-transaction fee a merchant pays its acquirer for card acceptance, of which interchange is one component?
explain: The MDR is paid by the merchant to its acquirer and then split into interchange fees, assessment (network) fees and processing fees; CRS notes it is typically around 1%-3% per transaction.
hook: MDR = the merchant's whole bill; interchange is the biggest slice.

sources.title: Mastercard Interchange Fees and Rates Explained | Mastercard US
sources.quote: Interchange fees are one component of the Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) established by acquirers, which is paid by merchants to acquirers in consideration for card acceptance services.

sources.title: Merchant Discount, Interchange, and Other Transaction Fees in the Retail Electronic Payment System | Congress.gov
sources.quote: For this service, the merchant agrees to pay a fee called the merchant discount rate (MDR) for each transaction. This fee is paid to the merchant's bank and then further split among the other market participants in the form of interchange fees, assessment fees, and payment processing fees, as described below. The MDR is typically around 1%-3% per transaction.

q: Which party in a card transaction receives scheme fees (also called assessment or network fees)?
explain: Scheme fees are the smaller slice of the merchant's fee that goes to the network such as Visa or Mastercard, as distinct from interchange (to the issuer) and acquirer margin.

sources.title: Merchant Discount, Interchange, and Other Transaction Fees in the Retail Electronic Payment System | Congress.gov
sources.quote: A smaller portion of the MDR goes to the network. This is sometimes referred to as a card brand, network access, or brand usage fee.

sources.title: MR22/1.10 scheme and processing fees final report - glossary
sources.quote: MSC Merchant service charge, which is the total amount merchants pay to acquirers for card-acquiring services. This comprises interchange fees, scheme and processing fees and acquirer net revenue.

q: Which Federal Reserve regulation implements the Durbin Amendment's debit card interchange fee limits?
explain: Regulation II (12 CFR part 235), issued in 2011, implements the Durbin Amendment by capping debit interchange for large issuers; credit card interchange is generally not covered.
hook: Reg II: two letters for the 'interchange' cap.

sources.title: 12 CFR PART 235—DEBIT CARD INTERCHANGE FEES AND ROUTING (REGULATION II)
sources.quote: 12 CFR PART 235—DEBIT CARD INTERCHANGE FEES AND ROUTING (REGULATION II)

sources.title: Merchant Discount, Interchange, and Other Transaction Fees in the Retail Electronic Payment System | Congress.gov
sources.quote: In 2011, the Federal Reserve issued Regulation II, implementing what is commonly known as the Durbin Amendment, which required the Fed to set debit interchange fees for large banks based on the cost of providing the services ... Credit card interchange is generally not covered by Regulation II.

q: Debit card issuers with assets below what threshold are exempt from Regulation II's interchange fee standards?
explain: The small-issuer exemption applies when the issuer, together with its affiliates, has assets of less than $10 billion as of the end of the preceding calendar year and holds the account debited.

sources.title: 12 CFR § 235.5 Exemptions.
sources.quote: (ii) The issuer, together with its affiliates, has assets of less than $10 billion as of the end of the calendar year preceding the date of the electronic debit transaction.

sources.title: The Fed - 2023 Interchange Fee Revenue, Covered Issuer Costs, and Covered Issuer and Merchant Fraud Losses Related to Debit Card Transactions
sources.quote: Additionally, an issuer with consolidated assets below $10 billion is not subject to the interchange fee standards, provided the issuer holds the account that is debited.

q: What is a card transaction completed online, by phone or by post, where the card is not physically presented to the merchant, called?
explain: A card-not-present (CNP) transaction includes e-commerce and mail or telephone orders; a card-present transaction is one where the cardholder presents the card at the merchant's outlet.
hook: Online = card not in the room.

sources.title: MR22/1.10 scheme and processing fees final report - glossary
sources.quote: Card-not-present (‘CNP') transaction A transaction that is completed online, by phone or by post, so a card (be it physical or tokenised) is not present when the merchant is taking payment.

sources.title: PSR Card acquiring market review - Final report - Glossary
sources.quote: Card-not-present transaction Any card transaction that is not a card-present transaction such as e-commerce transactions and mail order and telephone order transactions.

q: The chip card standard EMV is named after Europay, Mastercard and which other company?
explain: EMV originally came from Europay, Mastercard and Visa, the three companies that developed the original specifications and formed EMVCo.

sources.title: Why EMV? | EMVCo
sources.quote: The term EMV originally came from Europay, Mastercard and Visa, the three companies that collaborated to develop the original specifications and form EMVCo.

sources.title: Merchant Processing, Comptroller's Handbook
sources.quote: The technology was jointly developed by Europay, MasterCard, and Visa, and the technology is named for the original developers.

q: EMV Payment Tokenisation limits the risk of compromised use of which card data element by substituting a token for it?
explain: EMV Payment Tokenisation protects primary account numbers (PANs); a payment token should not be usable beyond a specific merchant, device or payment scenario.
hook: Token stands in for the PAN.

sources.title: EMV Payment Tokenisation | EMVCo
sources.quote: EMV ® Payment Tokenisation enhances the underlying security of digital payments by limiting the risk typically associated with compromised, unauthorised or fraudulent use of primary account numbers (PANs).

q: What is the reversal of a card transaction, initiated by the card issuer after a cardholder dispute, called?
explain: When a cardholder disputes a charge, the issuing bank reviews it and, if decided in the cardholder's favor, the payment is refunded to the customer and withdrawn from the merchant's account.
hook: Charge goes BACK to the cardholder.

sources.title: Chargebacks | Visa Acceptance Solutions | Visa
sources.quote: If the decision is in the customer’s favor, a chargeback is issued, meaning the payment is refunded to the customer and withdrawn from your account.

sources.title: Chargebacks: Another Payment Card Acceptance Cost for Merchants (Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City)
sources.quote: Chargebacks are full reversal of transactions by card issuers.

q: Which organization governs the U.S. ACH Network and develops its rules?
explain: Nacha governs the ACH Network and develops its rules and standards; the Federal Reserve and The Clearing House are the network's two ACH Operators.

sources.title: Same Day ACH Expansion to $1 Million Begins Today | Nacha
sources.quote: Nacha governs the thriving ACH Network, the payment system that drives safe, smart, and fast Direct Deposits and Direct Payments with the capability to reach all U.S. bank and credit union accounts. ... Nacha develops rules and standards, provides industry solutions, and delivers education, accreditation, and advisory services.

sources.title: ACH Payments Fact Sheet | Nacha
sources.quote: Nacha works cooperatively with the Federal Reserve and The Clearing House, as the two Operators of the modern ACH Network

q: Interoperator ACH payments between the Federal Reserve Banks and EPN are settled by whom?
explain: The Reserve Banks and EPN are the two national ACH operators and rely on each other for interoperator payments, which the Reserve Banks settle.
hook: Two operators, one settler: the Fed.

sources.title: Federal Reserve Board - Automated Clearinghouse Services
sources.quote: The Reserve Banks and Electronic Payments Network (EPN) are the two national ACH operators. ... These interoperator payments are settled by the Reserve Banks.

q: The Fedwire Funds Service is what type of settlement system?
explain: Fedwire Funds is an RTGS system provided by the Federal Reserve Banks; transfers are immediate, final and irrevocable once processed and it is generally used for large-value, time-critical payments.
hook: Wire = one at a time, final now.

sources.title: Federal Reserve Board - Fedwire Funds Services
sources.quote: The Federal Reserve Banks provide the Fedwire Funds Service, a real-time gross settlement system that enables participants to initiate funds transfer that are immediate, final, and irrevocable once processed.

sources.title: Fedwire Funds PFMI Disclosure - FRBservices.org
sources.quote: The Fedwire Funds Service is a real-time gross settlement system that enables participants to make final payments using their balances held at Reserve Banks or intraday credit provided by those Reserve Banks

q: Which company owns and operates the CHIPS large-value payment system?
explain: CHIPS is owned and operated by The Clearing House Payments Company L.L.C. and, unlike Fedwire, uses a liquidity-saving algorithm that nets some obligations.
hook: CHIPS is the private-sector wire; Fedwire is the Fed's.

sources.title: Fedwire Funds PFMI Disclosure - FRBservices.org
sources.quote: CHIPS is owned and operated by The Clearing House Payments Company L.L.C. CHIPS is not exclusively a gross settlement system. Instead, CHIPS processes some payment orders individually and others using a liquidity-saving algorithm that nets certain settlement obligations bilaterally or multilaterally.

sources.title: Our History | The Clearing House
sources.quote: The Payments Company is the only private-sector ACH and wire operator in the United States

q: In what year did The Clearing House launch its RTP real-time payments network?
explain: TCH launched RTP in November 2017, describing it as the first new core payments infrastructure in the U.S. in more than 40 years; it was built with technology from Vocalink, a Mastercard company.

sources.title: First New Core Payments System in the U.S. in more than 40 Years Initiates First Live Payments | The Clearing House
sources.quote: New York, NY (November 14, 2017) – Yesterday, The Clearing House (TCH) launched RTP®, its real-time payments system, the first new core payments infrastructure in the U.S. in more than 40 years.

sources.title: Bringing instant payments to the US | Mastercard Global
sources.quote: In 2016, Vocalink signed a contract with The Clearing House (TCH) to develop a national real-time payments service in the US. The RTP® network went live in November 2017.

q: In what year did the Federal Reserve's FedNow instant payment service go live?
explain: FedNow went live on July 20, 2023, offering 24x7x365 instant interbank clearing and settlement for U.S. depository institutions.

sources.title: Federal Reserve Board - FedNow Service
sources.quote: The FedNow Service went live on July 20, 2023.

sources.title: Federal Reserve announces that its new system for instant payments, the FedNow Service, is now live
sources.quote: The Federal Reserve on Thursday announced that its new system for instant payments, the FedNow ® Service, is now live.

q: Under Visa and Mastercard rules, what is a merchant that accepts cards through a payment facilitator called?
explain: A payment facilitator signs acceptance contracts with sponsored merchants (sub-merchants) on behalf of an acquirer and receives settlement on their behalf; the acquirer remains responsible for both.

sources.title: Visa Payment Facilitator Model
sources.quote: Signs a merchant acceptance contract with a sponsored merchant on behalf of an acquirer. ... A sponsored merchant is a merchant whose payment services are provided by a PF and all Visa merchant requirements apply equally to a sponsored merchant. Acquirers are responsible for the acts of both PFs and sponsored merchants.

sources.title: Transaction Processing Rules - Mastercard
sources.quote: Sponsored Merchant A merchant that, pursuant to an agreement with a Payment Facilitator, is authorized to accept Cards when properly presented. A Sponsored Merchant is also referred to as Submerchant.

q: In merchant acquiring, what does the abbreviation ISO stand for?
explain: ISOs sell card-acquiring services to merchants as agents on the acquirer's behalf; merchants that sign with an ISO are contracting with the acquirer.

sources.title: Beyond the Acquirer: Additional Visa Acceptance Entities
sources.quote: ISOs operate as agents on behalf of acquirers, meaning that when sellers sign services contracts with an ISO they are signing with the acquirer.

sources.title: PSR Card acquiring market review - Final report - Glossary
sources.quote: Independent sales organisation (ISO) An organisation that sells card-acquiring services to merchants on the acquirer’s behalf (alongside card acceptance products and value-added services ) but does not itself contract with merchants for card-acquiring services .

q: Under Visa's classification, an ISO that processes transactions is instead classified as what type of entity?
explain: Visa says ISOs do not process transactions, receive settlement funds or access cardholder data; an ISO that does process transactions is classified as a Third Party Servicer.
hook: Sell only = ISO; touch the processing = Third Party Servicer.

sources.title: Beyond the Acquirer: Additional Visa Acceptance Entities
sources.quote: Though ISOs may sell or resell gateway services in conjunction with selling the acquirer’s merchant account offering, ISOs do not process transactions, receive settlement funds, nor do they have access to the seller’s customer’s data or the transaction processing environment. If the ISO does, or intends to, process transactions, they will instead be classified as a Third Party Servicer.

q: What is the software that captures card details on a merchant's website and translates them into a message the acquirer's systems can understand?
explain: The UK Payment Systems Regulator defines a payment gateway as software that helps a merchant accept cards through a website by capturing and translating card details for the acquirer.
hook: Gateway = the online on-ramp to the acquirer.

sources.title: PSR Card acquiring market review - Final report - Glossary
sources.quote: Payment gateway Software that helps a merchant accept cards through a website by capturing the card details and translating them into a message that can be sent to and understood by the acquirer’s systems.

q: Under the CFPB's definition of a pay-in-four BNPL loan, the installments after the down payment are due at what interval?
explain: The CFPB defines BNPL as a four-installment, no-interest loan, typically with a 25 percent down payment at checkout and the remaining three installments due in two-week intervals over six weeks.
hook: Pay in 4 over 6 weeks = every 2 weeks.

sources.title: Buy Now, Pay Later: Market trends and consumer impacts (CFPB)
sources.quote: For purposes of this report, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) defines BNPL as the “pay-in-four” or “split pay” product: a four-installment, no-interest consumer loan, typically with a down payment of 25 percent and the remaining three installments due in two-week intervals.

sources.title: Buy Now, Pay Later: Policy Issues and Options for Congress | Congress.gov
sources.quote: One form of BNPL is the "Pay in 4" product, which is interest free and requires the first payment at the time of purchase and three additional purchases at two-week intervals over the next six weeks.

q: In what year was Bank of America's BankAmericard rebranded as Visa?
explain: Bank of America launched BankAmericard in California in 1958, spun it off into its own company in 1970, and it was rebranded as Visa in 1976.

sources.title: Electronic Point-of-Sale Payments | Federal Reserve History
sources.quote: The origins of the Visa network, for example, trace to 1958 when Bank of America launched BankAmericard in California. ... BankAmericard was spun off into its own company in 1970 and rebranded as Visa in 1976.

sources.title: First & Merchants BankAmericard Visa | National Museum of American History
sources.quote: In 1976 BankAmericard officially became branded as a Visa card.

q: Mastercard traces its roots to which bank association formed in 1966?
explain: In 1966 a group of banks formed the Interbank Card Association, which introduced the Master Charge brand and later became MasterCard International.

sources.title: Mastercard Inc. | History, Master Charge, IPO, & Facts | Britannica
sources.quote: It traces its roots to 1966, when a group of banks formed the Interbank Card Association to compete in the growing credit card market.

sources.title: Brand History | Mastercard US
sources.quote: In 1966, one of these groups formed the Interbank Card Association (ICA), which later became MasterCard International.

q: In what year did American Express introduce its Travelers Cheque?
explain: American Express, founded in 1850 as an express delivery company, introduced the Travelers Cheque in 1891 under president James C. Fargo.

sources.title: American Express Company | History & Facts | Britannica
sources.quote: On Fargo’s death in 1881, his younger brother, James Congdell Fargo (1829–1915), became president and guided the company for the next 33 years, introducing such innovations as the American Express Money Order (1882) and the American Express Travelers Cheque (1891)

sources.title: American Express History, Values, & Vision | About Amex
sources.quote: To help adventurous and entrepreneurial customers traveling abroad feel more secure with their money, we introduced the Travelers Cheque in 1891.

q: Approximately how much was eBay's 2002 acquisition of PayPal valued at?
explain: eBay completed its all-stock acquisition of PayPal on October 3, 2002, in a deal valued at approximately $1.5 billion; eBay later spun PayPal off in 2015.

sources.title: eBay Completes PayPal Acquisition (Exhibit 99.1, SEC.gov)
sources.quote: Based on eBay’s average closing stock price over the period two days before and after the acquisition was announced, the transaction is valued at approximately $1.5 billion.

sources.title: PayPal | History, Description, & Facts | Britannica Money
sources.quote: In October 2002, eBay acquired PayPal for $1.5 billion, making PayPal the official payments provider for eBay.

q: Who co-founded Stripe in 2010 with his brother John Collison?
explain: Patrick and John Collison started Stripe in 2010 to make it simpler to accept payments on the internet; Patrick is CEO and John is president.

sources.title: Patrick Collison Founder and CEO, Stripe (Congress.gov witness bio)
sources.quote: Patrick and his brother, John, started Stripe in 2010 with the goal of making it simpler to accept payments on the internet.

sources.title: Stripe co-founder and CEO Patrick Collison on "prizing the small details" - Haas News | UC Berkeley Haas
sources.quote: Patrick Collison and his brother John conceived of financial services company Stripe as something that they thought should already exist. ... And Stripe debuted in 2010
